# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

The organization has an opportunity to improve productivity, knowledge access, and employee experience by deploying a secure internal AI assistant across its 5,000-person workforce. Employees currently spend significant time searching for policies, locating institutional knowledge, summarizing documents, drafting routine communications, and navigating internal systems. Information is often distributed across collaboration platforms, document repositories, intranets, service portals, and line-of-business applications, creating inconsistent access and avoidable administrative work.

This project will deploy an enterprise AI assistant that provides employees with a conversational interface for finding trusted internal information, creating and refining workplace content, summarizing approved documents, and completing selected routine tasks. The assistant will operate within the organization’s security, privacy, records-management, and regulatory requirements. It will use role-based access controls and source citations so that employees receive answers grounded in content they are already authorized to access.

The initiative will be managed as a business transformation program rather than solely as a technology implementation. In addition to platform deployment and systems integration, the project will establish governance, define acceptable-use standards, prepare internal content, train employees, and create an operating model for ongoing improvement.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide all eligible employees with a secure, reliable, and easy-to-use AI assistant that reduces time spent on repetitive knowledge work and improves access to organizational information. The deployment is expected to shorten information-search cycles, accelerate drafting and summarization, improve consistency in routine communications, and reduce demand on shared-service teams for common questions.

The project will also establish a governed enterprise capability for generative AI. This includes clear accountability for platform ownership, data access, model risk, content quality, legal compliance, security monitoring, and responsible use. The assistant should complement employee judgment rather than replace it, with human review required for consequential decisions, external communications, and other high-risk activities.

A further objective is to create a scalable foundation for future use cases. The initial release will prioritize broadly applicable capabilities, while the technical architecture and governance model will support later integration with workflows such as IT support, HR services, finance operations, procurement, customer service, and project delivery.

## Scope

The project will select, configure, pilot, and deploy an enterprise AI assistant to the organization’s 5,000 employees. Core capabilities will include conversational question answering, enterprise search, document summarization, drafting and editing assistance, meeting and action-item synthesis where approved, and guided access to internal policies and procedures. Responses based on internal knowledge will include citations or links to source material wherever technically feasible.

The assistant will connect initially to a controlled set of high-value repositories, such as the corporate intranet, policy library, approved collaboration sites, document-management platform, IT knowledge base, and employee service portals. Integrations will preserve existing permissions so that the assistant cannot expose content a user is not authorized to view. Identity management, single sign-on, multifactor authentication, logging, retention, data-loss prevention, and security monitoring will be implemented through existing enterprise controls where possible.

The first release will support common, lower-risk use cases across the organization. It will not autonomously make employment, legal, financial, safety, compliance, or customer-impacting decisions. It will not send external communications, approve transactions, modify systems of record, or take actions on behalf of employees without explicit authorization and appropriate controls. Highly sensitive repositories and regulated data will remain out of scope until they have completed separate risk and control reviews.

The project also includes content readiness, employee communications, role-based training, an acceptable-use policy, support procedures, model and vendor risk assessments, and performance reporting. Custom autonomous agents, large-scale process automation, and extensive modernization of legacy repositories are outside the initial deployment, although selected high-value workflow integrations may be evaluated during the pilot.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment is expected to take approximately nine months, followed by ongoing optimization.

During the first six weeks, the project team will confirm business requirements, prioritize use cases, inventory data sources, evaluate platform options, and complete initial security, privacy, legal, accessibility, architecture, and procurement assessments. Baseline measurements will be collected for search time, service-request volumes, employee experience, and other target outcomes. The phase will conclude with platform selection, an approved business case, and a documented control framework.

From weeks seven through fourteen, the team will establish the technical foundation. Activities will include tenant or environment configuration, identity integration, permission testing, logging, data-loss prevention, retention settings, user-interface configuration, and connection of the first approved knowledge sources. In parallel, content owners will remove obsolete material, resolve conflicting policies, apply metadata, and assign accountability for maintaining authoritative sources.

A controlled pilot will run from weeks fifteen through twenty-two with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing different functions, locations, seniority levels, and accessibility needs. Pilot participants will receive practical training and structured use cases. The team will assess answer quality, citation accuracy, permission enforcement, user satisfaction, support demand, adoption patterns, and measurable time savings. Security testing, red-team exercises, privacy validation, and incident-response simulations will be completed before broad release.

Weeks twenty-three through thirty-four will cover staged enterprise rollout. Access will be expanded in waves, supported by executive sponsorship, manager toolkits, live demonstrations, self-service learning, office hours, and a network of departmental AI champions. Each wave will be reviewed against technical, security, adoption, and quality thresholds before the next begins. High-value knowledge sources will be added progressively rather than connected all at once.

During the final four weeks of the initial program, the project team will stabilize operations, resolve priority issues, validate benefits, and transition the service to its permanent owners. A twelve-month enhancement roadmap will then be approved, covering additional repositories, workflow integrations, departmental use cases, and improvements identified through analytics and user feedback.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require an executive sponsor with authority to resolve cross-functional issues and maintain alignment with organizational strategy. A full-time program manager will coordinate delivery, dependencies, budget, risk, communications, and benefits realization. A product owner will manage the assistant’s roadmap, prioritize use cases, and represent employee needs.

The core implementation team should include an enterprise architect, two to four AI or application engineers, two integration engineers, a data or search engineer, a security architect, a privacy representative, a legal and compliance representative, an identity and access-management specialist, and quality-assurance support. Content onboarding will require a knowledge-management lead and part-time content owners from each participating function. Change and adoption activities will require a change manager, communications support, learning-design capacity, and approximately 50 to 100 trained AI champions distributed across the organization.

Operational support should use a tiered model. The existing service desk can provide first-line assistance after training, while a small specialist team handles answer-quality issues, access problems, connector failures, safety concerns, and vendor escalations. Permanent service ownership is likely to require a product manager, two platform or AI engineers, a knowledge manager, an adoption lead, and shared support from security, privacy, legal, records management, and enterprise architecture.

Budget requirements will include software licensing or model consumption, implementation services, integration development, security and compliance tooling, content remediation, training, communications, support, and contingency. Final costs will depend on the selected platform and consumption model. The business case should model three-year total cost of ownership, including recurring licenses, usage growth, repository connectors, support staffing, and future integration costs. A contingency of approximately 10 to 15 percent should be reserved for remediation, additional controls, and unplanned integration work.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

The organization will establish an AI governance group accountable for approving use cases, setting risk thresholds, monitoring performance, and reviewing incidents. Membership should include technology, security, privacy, legal, compliance, records management, HR, accessibility, internal audit, and business representatives. The group will maintain the acceptable-use policy, approve material changes, and oversee periodic risk reviews.

The assistant will follow least-privilege access principles and inherit source-system permissions. Internal data will not be used to train public models, and vendor contractual terms must provide appropriate protections for data ownership, confidentiality, data location, retention, subprocessors, and deletion. Prompts and outputs will be logged and retained only to the extent justified by operational, legal, and security requirements. Sensitive-data controls will be tested before launch and monitored continuously.

Employees will be informed that AI-generated content may be incomplete or incorrect. The user experience will encourage source verification and human review, particularly for legal, financial, personnel, compliance, safety, and external-facing content. The organization will provide a clear mechanism for reporting inaccurate, biased, unsafe, or improperly disclosed information, with defined triage and escalation procedures.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to at least 95 percent of eligible employees, maintains agreed availability and response-time service levels, and passes all required security, privacy, legal, accessibility, and compliance reviews. Permission testing must demonstrate that users cannot retrieve content beyond their existing authorization, with no unresolved critical security findings at enterprise launch.

Within three months of full deployment, the organization should target at least 60 percent employee activation and 40 percent monthly active use, with adoption distributed across functions rather than concentrated in a small number of teams. At least 75 percent of surveyed active users should report that the assistant is useful, and at least 70 percent should indicate that it helps them complete common tasks more efficiently.

Quality will be measured through a benchmark set of representative questions and tasks. The assistant should produce grounded, relevant answers for at least 85 percent of approved knowledge queries, provide valid citations for at least 90 percent of responses that rely on internal sources, and keep confirmed material-error rates below an agreed threshold. Critical permission failures or harmful disclosures will have zero tolerance and will trigger immediate containment and review.

The project should demonstrate measurable operational value within six months of enterprise rollout. Target outcomes include a 20 percent reduction in time spent searching for internal information, a 15 percent reduction in selected repetitive service-desk or shared-service inquiries, and average self-reported savings of at least one hour per active user per week. Benefits will be validated through usage analytics, time studies, service data, employee surveys, and selected departmental case studies rather than relying on anecdotal evidence alone.

Long-term success will be demonstrated by sustained adoption, improving answer quality, controlled expansion into valuable workflows, and a transparent governance process that maintains employee trust. Quarterly reviews will compare realized benefits with total operating costs and will guide decisions to expand, modify, or retire individual capabilities.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization will create a common, secure interface for knowledge and routine workplace assistance while establishing the controls needed for responsible enterprise use of generative AI. A phased nine-month implementation will allow the organization to validate value, manage risk, prepare its information assets, and build employee confidence before full deployment. With strong executive sponsorship, disciplined governance, representative piloting, and measurable outcome tracking, the program can deliver meaningful productivity gains and provide a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled services.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

Employees across the organization spend significant time searching for information, navigating policies, drafting routine content, summarizing documents, and completing repetitive administrative tasks. Relevant knowledge is distributed across intranets, document repositories, collaboration platforms, service portals, and departmental systems, creating delays and inconsistent answers. Public generative AI tools may improve productivity, but their unmanaged use introduces risks involving confidential information, privacy, security, intellectual property, and regulatory compliance.

This project will deploy a secure internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The assistant will provide a governed conversational interface for finding trusted internal information, producing and refining workplace content, summarizing approved materials, and supporting selected business workflows. It will use enterprise identity controls, permission-aware retrieval, audit logging, data-loss protections, and human oversight. The program will begin with a controlled pilot and expand in phases based on measured value, safety, and user readiness.

## Objectives

The project’s primary objective is to improve employee productivity by reducing the time required to find information and complete common knowledge-work tasks. The assistant will make approved organizational knowledge easier to access while preserving the source systems’ existing permissions and presenting citations so users can verify responses.

The project will also establish a safe alternative to unmanaged public AI services. It will introduce organization-wide standards for acceptable use, privacy, security, model governance, content ownership, human review, and incident handling. In addition, the program will build reusable technical and operating capabilities that allow business units to introduce new AI-supported use cases without creating separate, inconsistent solutions.

Within the first year, the organization aims to achieve broad employee adoption, measurable time savings, improved access to trusted information, and no material breach of confidential data attributable to the platform.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide employees with a secure web-based assistant integrated with the organization’s single sign-on and role-based access controls. Where technically and commercially appropriate, the assistant will also be available within existing productivity and collaboration tools.

Core capabilities will include general drafting and editing, document and meeting summarization, translation where approved, brainstorming, and question answering grounded in authorized internal sources. Initial knowledge connections will prioritize high-value, broadly applicable content such as human resources policies, information technology guidance, operating procedures, benefits information, communications standards, and selected departmental knowledge bases. Responses based on internal content will include links or citations to source material and will respect document-level permissions.

The project will include platform selection or configuration, systems integration, security and privacy assessments, data classification, knowledge preparation, testing, policy development, user training, support processes, adoption communications, analytics, and ongoing model evaluation. Initial workflow integrations may include IT and HR self-service, subject to validation and approval by the relevant process owners.

The first release will not permit fully autonomous decisions, unsupervised external communications, or actions that create material legal, financial, employment, safety, or customer impact. High-risk uses—including employment decisions, legal conclusions, financial approvals, regulated advice, and processing of specially restricted data—will remain out of scope unless separately assessed and approved. The assistant will augment employees rather than replace accountable human judgment, and users will remain responsible for reviewing outputs before relying on or distributing them.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program will be delivered over approximately twelve months, followed by continuous improvement.

During months one and two, the project team will confirm priority use cases, document requirements, establish governance, classify relevant data, evaluate platform options, and define the target architecture. Security, privacy, legal, records-management, procurement, accessibility, and works council or labor considerations will be addressed during this phase. Baseline measures will be collected for search time, service volumes, employee experience, and existing use of public AI tools.

During months three and four, the team will configure the platform and its identity, logging, monitoring, data-protection, and administrative controls. Initial knowledge repositories will be connected, and content owners will remove obsolete or duplicated materials, assign authoritative sources, and confirm access permissions. Evaluation datasets will be created to test answer quality, citation accuracy, permission enforcement, harmful content, prompt injection, and data leakage.

A pilot will run during months five and six with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing multiple functions, locations, job types, and levels of technical confidence. Participants will receive role-based training and clear acceptable-use guidance. The team will measure task completion, answer quality, time savings, user satisfaction, support demand, and safety incidents. Critical issues will be resolved before wider deployment.

During months seven through nine, access will expand to approximately 2,000 employees. Additional high-value knowledge sources will be introduced, support processes will be scaled, and departmental champions will help employees identify appropriate use cases. Any workflow integration will pass security, operational, and business-owner acceptance testing before release.

During months ten through twelve, the assistant will be made available to all eligible employees. Enterprise communications, self-service learning, manager toolkits, office hours, and a structured champion network will support adoption. At the end of the period, the steering committee will review results against the success criteria and approve the ongoing roadmap, budget, and operating model.

Deployment gates will require documented approval from security, privacy, legal, technology, and business owners. Expansion may be paused if evaluation thresholds are not met or if unresolved risks exceed the organization’s tolerance.

## Resource Requirements

Executive sponsorship should be provided by a senior leader with authority across technology and business functions. A cross-functional steering committee should include representatives from information technology, cybersecurity, data and AI governance, legal, privacy, human resources, communications, records management, risk, procurement, accessibility, and participating business units.

The core delivery team is expected to require approximately 12 to 16 full-time-equivalent roles during implementation. This includes a program manager, product manager, enterprise architect, two to four AI or machine-learning engineers, two integration engineers, a security engineer, a data or knowledge architect, a user-experience specialist, a change and communications lead, a training lead, a business analyst, and service-management support. Legal, privacy, compliance, procurement, accessibility, and content-owner contributions may be part-time but must be formally allocated. Each participating function should nominate a knowledge owner and one or more AI champions.

Technology requirements include an enterprise AI platform, approved model access, secure hosting, identity and access management, retrieval and indexing services, encryption, data-loss prevention, content filtering, audit logging, monitoring, analytics, evaluation tooling, and integration capacity for selected repositories and applications. The architecture should support model replacement, retention controls, regional data requirements, usage quotas, disaster recovery, and separation of development, testing, and production environments.

The project budget should cover platform and model consumption fees, implementation services, integration work, security testing, content remediation, training, communications, support, and contingency. A planning estimate of $2.5 million to $4 million for the first year is appropriate, subject to vendor selection, existing licenses, usage levels, integration complexity, and hosting requirements. Ongoing annual costs are expected to include software licensing or consumption, a permanent product and engineering team of approximately six to ten full-time equivalents, service-desk capacity, security monitoring, content governance, training, and periodic independent assurance.

## Governance and Risk Management

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI policy defining approved uses, prohibited activities, accountability, human-review requirements, data-handling rules, and escalation procedures. A risk-based intake process will evaluate new knowledge sources, capabilities, and workflow integrations before release. Material changes to models, prompts, security controls, or data connections will require testing and documented approval.

The platform will apply least-privilege access, encryption, retention controls, permission-aware retrieval, data-loss prevention, and comprehensive audit logging. Enterprise data will not be used to train external models unless explicitly authorized by contract and governance. The organization will maintain procedures for reporting incorrect or harmful answers, privacy concerns, unauthorized disclosure, intellectual-property issues, and service outages. Regular testing will assess hallucination, bias, prompt injection, inappropriate content, permission leakage, and performance degradation.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful if it delivers measurable employee value while remaining within approved risk tolerances. By the end of the first year, at least 70 percent of eligible employees should have activated the assistant, at least 50 percent should use it monthly, and at least 30 percent should use it weekly. User satisfaction should reach at least 80 percent among active users, and at least 75 percent should report that the assistant helps them complete relevant work more efficiently.

Controlled studies and user surveys should demonstrate an average time saving of at least 60 minutes per active user per week for supported tasks. For selected HR and IT information requests, the organization should achieve a 15 to 25 percent reduction in routine service contacts or handling time without reducing service quality.

For approved benchmark questions, at least 85 percent of grounded answers should be rated correct, useful, and supported by valid citations. Permission testing must demonstrate that users cannot retrieve content they are not authorized to access, with all critical access-control tests passing before each rollout stage. The program should have no material confidential-data breach attributable to the assistant and no unresolved critical security or privacy finding at launch.

Operationally, the service should maintain at least 99.5 percent availability after enterprise rollout, resolve critical incidents within agreed service levels, and review high-risk feedback promptly. All connected knowledge domains must have named owners and documented review schedules, and all employees must complete required AI-use training before receiving access.

A benefits and risk report will be presented to the steering committee quarterly. Continued investment will depend on sustained adoption, verified productivity gains, acceptable answer quality, effective governance, and evidence that the platform is reducing—not increasing—organizational risk.

## Recommendation

The organization should authorize the twelve-month phased program and fund the discovery and foundation stage immediately. A controlled rollout will allow the organization to capture near-term productivity benefits while establishing the technical, governance, and workforce capabilities required for responsible enterprise AI adoption.

Baseline measures will be collected for search time, service request volume, employee experience, and representative task completion times.

During months three and four, the team will configure the core environment, implement single sign-on and role-based access, establish logging and monitoring, connect the initial knowledge sources, and define retention, content filtering, and incident response controls. A representative evaluation set will be created to test answer accuracy, citation quality, security boundaries, bias, and resistance to prompt-based attacks.

During months five and six, a controlled pilot will be conducted with approximately 250 to 500 employees across several functions and job levels. Pilot participants will receive role-based training and structured opportunities to provide feedback. The project team will evaluate usability, response quality, data leakage risks, adoption patterns, and productivity impact. Critical issues will be resolved before broader release.

During months seven through nine, the service will expand to approximately 2,000 employees. Additional approved knowledge sources and high-value use cases will be introduced, and a network of departmental AI champions will support adoption. Communications, training, office hours, and manager guidance will reinforce appropriate use and human accountability.

During months ten through twelve, the assistant will be made available to the remaining eligible workforce. The team will complete operational handover, publish service-level expectations, confirm the long-term funding model, and establish a prioritized roadmap for new integrations and department-specific capabilities. A formal benefits review will determine whether the program should proceed to more advanced workflow automation.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative requires a dedicated cross-functional team with clear business and technical ownership. Executive sponsorship should be shared by a senior business leader and the Chief Information Officer or equivalent. Day-to-day delivery should be led by a full-time program manager and product manager, supported by an enterprise architect, two to four AI or software engineers, two integration or data engineers, a security engineer, and platform administration capacity.

Part-time participation will be required from privacy, legal, compliance, records management, procurement, human resources, internal communications, learning and development, accessibility, and employee relations. Each participating business function should appoint a subject-matter owner to validate content and use cases. A change lead, training specialist, service designer, data analyst, and two support specialists should be assigned during pilot and rollout. A network of approximately 50 to 100 trained AI champions—roughly one for every 50 to 100 employees—will provide local guidance and collect feedback.

Technology requirements include enterprise AI platform licenses, model consumption capacity, secure cloud infrastructure, integration tooling, identity and access management, content indexing, monitoring, audit logging, analytics, data-loss prevention, and testing tools. Funding should also cover implementation support, employee training, security testing, accessibility review, and contingency capacity for usage growth. The final budget will depend on platform selection and consumption levels, but planning should distinguish one-time implementation costs from recurring licenses, model usage, support, and governance expenses.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

A cross-functional AI governance committee will approve use cases, data sources, risk classifications, and material changes to the service. The assistant will follow the principles of least privilege, data minimization, transparency, and human accountability. Employee prompts and generated content will be handled according to documented retention and monitoring rules, and enterprise data will not be used to train external models unless explicitly authorized by contract and policy.

Responses grounded in internal information should provide citations or links to source material wherever practical. The interface will remind employees that outputs may be incomplete or incorrect and must be reviewed before consequential use. Automated evaluations, human testing, red-team exercises, access reviews, and incident reporting will be incorporated into the operating model. The service will also be designed and tested for accessibility and equitable use across employee groups.

## Change Management and Adoption

Successful deployment will depend on employee trust and practical relevance. Communications will explain what the assistant can do, what it cannot do, how employee data is handled, and when human judgment is required. Training will use realistic role-based examples rather than generic demonstrations and will cover effective prompting, source verification, confidentiality, intellectual property, bias, and escalation procedures.

Managers will receive guidance on integrating the assistant into work without treating usage volume as an employee performance measure. AI champions, office hours, short learning modules, prompt libraries, and in-product guidance will help employees build confidence. Feedback mechanisms will allow users to flag incorrect, unsafe, outdated, or unhelpful responses, with defined ownership for review and remediation.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful if the assistant is deployed to at least 90 percent of eligible employees by the end of month twelve, with at least 60 percent of eligible employees using it monthly and at least 35 percent using it weekly within three months of full rollout. In post-deployment measurement, active users should report an average time saving of at least one hour per week, and representative tasks should show a 20 percent or greater reduction in completion time without a decline in quality.

For grounded question-answering use cases, at least 85 percent of evaluated responses should be correct, relevant, and supported by valid citations, with higher thresholds applied to sensitive domains. The service should achieve at least 99.5 percent availability after stabilization and meet agreed response-time targets. User satisfaction should reach at least 75 percent favorable, and at least 80 percent of employees granted access should complete required responsible-use training.

The deployment must produce no confirmed material disclosure of restricted information caused by a failure of the assistant’s access controls. High-severity security, privacy, or compliance findings must be remediated before expansion to the next rollout stage. The program should also demonstrate measurable operational benefits, such as a reduction in repetitive internal support requests, faster retrieval of policy and process information, or improved turnaround time for selected knowledge-work activities. Results will be reviewed quarterly, and continued investment will depend on sustained value, acceptable risk, and evidence that the service is improving employee outcomes.

## Expected Outcome

At completion, the organization will have a secure, governed, and broadly adopted internal AI assistant supported by a repeatable operating model. Employees will have faster access to trusted information and practical assistance with everyday work, while the organization will gain centralized oversight of AI usage, stronger protection of enterprise data, and a foundation for future automation. The phased approach will allow the organization to realize near-term productivity gains without compromising security, compliance, or human accountability.

For a consumer-facing AI agent with a **50 ms end-to-end latency budget**, choose **AKS**, using dedicated node pools, pre-warmed replicas, topology-aware routing, and regional/private dependencies. Azure Container Apps is operationally simpler, but its abstraction, scale-to-zero behavior, and reduced infrastructure control make consistently meeting a hard 50 ms target more difficult.

Both options can support data residency if deployed in an approved Azure region, but validate where logs, model endpoints, registries, backups, and monitoring data are stored—not just the application containers.

### Three trade-offs

1. **Latency control vs. operational burden**  
   - **AKS:** Greater control over node placement, VM types, networking, autoscaling, ingress, and warm capacity; better for predictable tail latency.  
   - **Container Apps:** Less administration, but cold starts and platform-managed scheduling/networking can increase p95/p99 variability.

2. **Elasticity vs. cost efficiency**  
   - **Container Apps:** Excellent for unpredictable diurnal traffic, including rapid event-driven scaling and scale-to-zero.  
   - **AKS:** Requires tuning cluster/node autoscalers and maintaining headroom. Keeping replicas warm to meet 50 ms raises off-peak cost.

3. **Residency/governance control vs. simplicity**

   - **Container Apps:** Can meet many residency requirements, but offers less control and requires confirmation that all managed-service metadata and telemetry remain within permitted boundaries.

### Migration risk

Moving later from Container Apps to AKS may expose dependencies on Container Apps-specific ingress, revisions, secrets, identity, and KEDA scaling semantics. This can cause behavioral differences—especially autoscaling lag and tail-latency regressions—so keep deployment manifests, identity, telemetry, and scaling configuration portable from the outset.

### Most likely causes

1. **Iteration through an unordered container**  
   Records are accumulated in a `set`, hash map, or grouped structure and then emitted by its iteration order.

2. **Nondeterministic input or concurrent processing**  
   The input comes from a database query without `ORDER BY`, filesystem enumeration, or parallel workers whose completion order varies.

3. **Unstable duplicate selection**  
   An unstable sort, incomplete comparator, or concurrent map overwrite makes it unpredictable which record wins when composite keys are equal.

### Stable, order-preserving implementation

This version keeps the **first occurrence** of each composite key and preserves input order:

```python
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
K = TypeVar("K")


def deduplicate(
    records: Iterable[T],
    key: Callable[[T], K],
) -> list[T]:
    seen: set[K] = set()
    result: list[T] = []

    for record in records:
        composite_key = key(record)

        if composite_key not in seen:
            seen.add(composite_key)
            result.append(record)

    return result
```

Example:

```python
records = [
    {"account_id": 1, "date": "2026-09-10", "value": "first"},
    {"account_id": 2, "date": "2026-09-10", "value": "other"},
    {"account_id": 1, "date": "2026-09-10", "value": "duplicate"},
]

unique = deduplicate(
    records,
    key=lambda r: (r["account_id"], r["date"]),
)
```

`unique` contains the first and second records, in their original order. For reproducibility, the input itself must also have deterministic ordering—for example, use an explicit `ORDER BY` when loading records from a database.

| Dimension | Fine-tuned small model | Prompt-engineered large model |
|---|---|---|
| **Quality** | Strong fit for a narrow classification task. With 40,000 labeled examples, it can learn domain terminology and decision boundaries directly. Likely more consistent output formatting and easier calibration. | May perform well immediately and handle ambiguous cases better, but prompting alone does not fully exploit the labeled dataset. | **Latency** | Best path to a reliable **60 ms target**, especially with an encoder/classification model, batching, quantization, and deployment near the application. | A large hosted model will often exceed 60 ms from network and generation latency alone. Self-hosting could reduce latency but requires costly accelerators and aggressive optimization. |
| **Cost** | Upfront training and evaluation expense, followed by low and predictable per-request inference cost. Particularly attractive at moderate or high volume. | Little initial training cost, but higher recurring token/API or GPU expense. However, runtime behavior and capacity planning are controllable. | Faster prototype and less ML training infrastructure with a hosted API, but introduces vendor dependency, rate limits, model-version changes, prompt regression testing, and less predictable latency/cost. | **Reliability** | Fixed label set, deterministic inference, straightforward confidence thresholds, and easier error analysis. | Must constrain and validate generated responses. Occasional malformed or unsupported labels remain possible unless structured-output controls are robust. |
| **Adaptability** | Changes require additional labels and retraining, though 40,000 examples provide a strong starting point. | New instructions or labels can sometimes be introduced by changing the prompt, making rapid experimentation easier. |

### Recommendation

**Fine-tune a small model**, preferably a compact encoder or classification-specific architecture rather than a small generative model.

The decisive factors are:

1. **40,000 labels are enough to make supervised fine-tuning highly effective.**
2. **The 60 ms latency target strongly disfavors a large-model API.**
3. **Small-model inference provides more predictable costs under a fixed monthly budget.**
4. **Classification does not usually justify paying for the broad generative capabilities of a large model.**

Use a stratified train/validation/test split, optimize for the business metric rather than accuracy alone, calibrate confidence scores, and benchmark p95/p99 latency on target hardware. Quantization or ONNX/TensorRT-style optimization can provide additional headroom. If some low-confidence cases are unusually difficult, an optional large-model fallback can be added later, subject to a strict traffic and budget cap.

**Fine-tune a small model.**

The combination of **40,000 labeled examples**, a strict **60 ms latency target**, and a **fixed monthly budget** strongly favors specialization over general-purpose model capability. Use a compact pretrained encoder or similarly small classifier, then apply quantization and deploy on dedicated CPU/GPU infrastructure as needed.

A practical process:

1. Build a prompted large-model baseline to establish an accuracy ceiling and inspect difficult examples.

3. If needed, use the large model only as an offline labeling/error-analysis tool or as a tightly budgeted fallback for low-confidence cases.

# Technical Brief: Deterministic vs. Learned Model Routing

## 1. Overview

Model routing selects which model handles each request.

- **Deterministic policy-based routing:** Uses explicit rules based on request metadata, task type, tenant, latency budget, token count, risk level, or other known signals.
- **Learned automatic routing:** Uses a classifier, scoring model, bandit, or reinforcement-learning system to predict the cheapest model likely to meet a quality target.

## 2. Comparison

| Dimension | Deterministic Policy-Based Routing | Learned Automatic Routing |
|---|---|---|
| **Controllability** | High. Decisions are explainable, reproducible, and constrained by explicit policy. Easy to enforce tenant, compliance, and model-eligibility rules. | Lower unless tightly constrained. Behavior depends on training data, thresholds, and distribution stability. Per-request decisions may be difficult to explain. |
| **Cost predictability** | High. Traffic allocation and unit economics can be estimated directly from rule frequencies and model prices. | Potentially more cost-efficient, but less predictable. Small threshold or traffic-distribution changes can shift substantial volume to expensive models. |
| **Quality optimization** | Coarse. Rules may over-route simple requests or under-route unusual difficult ones. | More granular. Can exploit semantic and contextual signals to assign the least expensive model expected to satisfy the quality target. |
| **Adaptability** | Requires manual rule changes and testing. Stable but slower to respond to new tasks or model changes. | Can adapt through retraining or online learning, but introduces model lifecycle, drift, and feedback-loop risks. |
| **Operational complexity** | Low to moderate. Requires policy versioning, simulation, and conflict resolution. | High. Requires labeled outcomes, calibration, retraining, drift monitoring, safe deployment, and exploration controls. |
| **Latency overhead** | Usually negligible. | Adds router inference latency and potentially feature-computation or embedding costs. |
| **Auditability** | Strong. A decision can normally be traced to a specific rule and policy version. | Weaker unless prediction scores, features, model versions, and explanations are recorded. |
| **Handling novel inputs** | Predictable defaults, but limited semantic generalization. | May generalize better, but confidence can be unreliable out of distribution. |

## 3. Failure Modes

### Deterministic routing

Common failures include:

- **Rule gaps:** New request types match no specialized route.
- **Rule overlap or precedence errors:** Multiple policies apply, producing unintended routing.
- **Brittle heuristics:** Token count or keywords poorly approximate task difficulty.
- **Stale configuration:** Pricing, model capabilities, or workload patterns change without policy updates.
- **Traffic cliffs:** A hard threshold sends similar requests to models with very different cost or quality.
- **Combinatorial complexity:** Rules become difficult to maintain across tenants, regions, models, and risk classes.

Mitigations include typed policy schemas, explicit precedence, policy simulation against historical traffic, canary releases, and mandatory default routes.

### Learned routing

Common failures include:

- **Distribution drift:** Production traffic differs from router training data.
- **Miscalibration:** The router is overconfident that a cheaper model will succeed.
- **Label leakage or weak labels:** Training targets do not represent actual production quality.
- **Feedback loops:** Requests routed to cheaper models generate the data used to justify continued cheap routing.
- **Optimization mismatch:** The router minimizes model cost while ignoring retries, latency, abandonment, or downstream correction costs.
- **Correlated failure:** Both the router and selected model fail on the same unfamiliar input class.
- **Unbounded escalation:** Conservative thresholds route too much traffic to premium models.
- **Silent quality degradation:** Aggregate metrics remain stable while specific languages, tenants, or task categories regress.

Mitigations include calibrated confidence estimates, out-of-distribution detection, hard routing constraints, shadow evaluation, stratified quality monitoring, and caps on premium-model allocation.

## 4. Observability Requirements

Both approaches should record:

- Request category and relevant non-sensitive features
- Selected model and candidate models
- Router and policy version
- Decision reason
- Estimated and actual token usage, latency, and cost
- Retries, escalations, timeouts, and fallback path
- Quality signals segmented by tenant, task, language, and risk class

Additional requirements differ:

### Policy-based routing

Log:

- Matched rule and precedence chain
- Default-route frequency
- Rule-level traffic, cost, latency, and quality
- Counterfactual results from offline replay when policies change

### Learned routing

Log:

- Prediction scores and confidence
- Feature and calibration versions
- Thresholds active at decision time
- Out-of-distribution indicators
- Expected versus realized quality and cost
- Traffic allocation by score band
- Drift and subgroup performance metrics

Learned routing should also support **shadow mode**, where its proposed decisions are recorded without controlling production traffic, and **counterfactual evaluation** using randomized or carefully designed holdout samples.

## 5. Fallback Strategy

A robust fallback chain should be independent of the primary routing method:

1. **Enforce hard eligibility constraints first**  
   Exclude models that violate compliance, residency, modality, context-window, or tenant requirements.

2. **Select the primary model**  
   Apply deterministic policy or the learned router within the eligible set.

3. **Detect failure explicitly**  
   Trigger fallback on timeout, provider error, malformed output, failed validation, low confidence, safety rejection, or task-specific quality checks.

4. **Retry selectively**  
   Retry transient infrastructure errors with bounded exponential backoff. Avoid repeating semantic failures against the same model and prompt unchanged.

5. **Escalate by capability**  
   Route to a stronger model when validation fails or confidence is below threshold. Cap escalation attempts and total cost.

6. **Use provider and regional redundancy**  
   Maintain an alternate provider or deployment for availability failures, subject to compliance constraints.

7. **Degrade gracefully**  
   For noncritical workloads, return a limited response, queue asynchronous processing, or disable expensive optional features rather than escalating indefinitely.

8. **Apply circuit breakers**  
   Remove unhealthy or unexpectedly expensive models from eligibility and switch to a known-safe static policy.

## 6. Recommendation for a Cost-Sensitive, High-Volume Workload

Use a **hybrid architecture with deterministic controls and a learned optimizer inside those controls**.

Recommended design:

- Route well-understood, high-volume request classes using deterministic rules to inexpensive models.
- Reserve premium models for explicitly high-risk or high-value categories.
- Use a calibrated learned router only for ambiguous requests where semantic difficulty prediction can produce meaningful savings.
- Constrain the learned router with:
  - Model allowlists
  - Per-tenant and global cost budgets
  - Minimum quality thresholds
  - Premium-model traffic caps
  - Out-of-distribution fallback to a safe deterministic route
- Validate outputs where possible and escalate only on concrete failure signals.
- Deploy the learned router in shadow mode, then canary it on a small traffic percentage.
- Maintain a one-command or automatic rollback to deterministic routing.
- Optimize **total cost per successful request**, including router inference, retries, escalation, latency, and downstream correction—not merely initial model price.

### Bottom line

For a cost-sensitive production system, fully automatic learned routing creates unnecessary financial and operational risk unless routing quality can be measured reliably. Deterministic routing provides the best baseline for control, auditability, and budget predictability. A constrained learned router can then improve efficiency at the margins without being allowed to override compliance, reliability, or spending limits.

# Technical Brief: Deterministic vs. Learned Model Routing

## 1. Overview

**Deterministic policy-based routing** selects a model using explicit rules, such as request type, tenant tier, token count, latency target, geography, or safety classification.

**Learned automatic routing** uses a trained classifier, scoring model, bandit, or reinforcement-learning policy to predict which model will satisfy a request at the lowest cost or best quality-cost tradeoff.

## 2. Comparison

| Dimension | Deterministic Policy-Based Routing | Learned Automatic Routing |
|---|---|---|
| **Controllability** | High. Decisions follow explicit, reviewable rules. Easy to impose budgets, compliance restrictions, model allowlists, and tenant-specific policies. | Lower unless constrained. Behavior depends on training data, objective design, calibration, and distribution stability. Hard constraints must be implemented outside the learned router. |
| **Cost predictability** | High. Traffic allocation and model prices can be modeled directly. Worst-case spend is easier to bound with quotas and routing caps. | Potentially more cost-efficient, but less predictable. Small changes in scores or traffic mix can shift substantial volume to expensive models. Requires budget constraints and continuous monitoring. |
| **Quality optimization** | Coarse-grained. Rules may overuse expensive models or send difficult requests to weak models because they cannot capture subtle semantic difficulty. | Fine-grained. Can estimate task difficulty and route individual requests based on expected quality, latency, and cost. Benefits depend on representative labels and reliable evaluation. |
| **Failure modes** | Rule gaps, incorrect precedence, brittle thresholds, configuration drift, and unhandled combinations. Failures are usually reproducible and localized. | Misclassification, poor calibration, data drift, feedback loops, reward gaming, correlated routing errors, and silent degradation. Failures may be probabilistic and difficult to reproduce. |
| **Observability** | Straightforward. Log the matched rule, policy version, inputs, and selected model. Decisions are readily explainable. | More demanding. Requires scores, confidence, feature values, router version, calibration metrics, and counterfactual evaluation. A model choice may not have a simple human-readable explanation. |
| **Change management** | Policy changes can be reviewed, tested, staged, and rolled back like configuration or code. | Updates require data validation, retraining or recalibration, offline evaluation, canarying, and drift monitoring. Rollback should include both model and feature-pipeline versions. |
| **Operational complexity** | Low to moderate. Complexity grows as rules accumulate and interact. | High. Adds a training pipeline, labels, feature availability, model serving, experimentation, monitoring, and governance. |
| **Adaptability** | Limited. New request patterns require explicit rule changes. | Stronger. Can exploit patterns not captured by manual policies, assuming the training and feedback processes remain representative. |

## 3. Failure Modes and Mitigations

### Deterministic routing

Common failures:

- Missing or overlapping rules
- Incorrect rule precedence
- Brittle token-count or keyword thresholds
- Configuration drift across environments
- Policy growth that becomes difficult to reason about
- Static rules failing to reflect model or traffic changes

Mitigations:

- Define a total ordering and a default route
- Validate policies with schema and conflict checks
- Maintain request-corpus regression tests
- Version all policies and support immediate rollback
- Shadow-test changes against production traffic
- Track routing distribution by rule, tenant, task type, and model

### Learned routing

Common failures:

- Router confidence is poorly calibrated
- Training data does not represent production traffic
- Distribution drift changes routing behavior
- Optimizing proxy metrics harms actual task quality
- Feedback loops bias future training data
- Feature-pipeline failures cause widespread misrouting
- Exploration mechanisms create unexpected spend or quality regressions

Mitigations:

- Enforce hard policy and budget constraints outside the router
- Use abstention thresholds for low-confidence decisions
- Monitor calibration, drift, quality, cost, and route distribution
- Evaluate against fixed holdout and adversarial test sets
- Run shadow and canary deployments before increasing traffic
- Limit how much traffic can move between model tiers per release
- Preserve deterministic fallback behavior

## 4. Observability Requirements

Both approaches should log:

- Request and tenant class, with sensitive data removed
- Selected model and model version
- Routing policy or router version
- Estimated and actual input/output tokens
- Latency, retries, errors, and final disposition
- Estimated and actual cost
- Quality signals where available
- Fallback events and reasons

Additional requirements for deterministic routing:

- Matched rule ID
- Rule evaluation trace
- Default-route usage
- Rule conflict or validation warnings

Additional requirements for learned routing:

- Candidate-model scores
- Confidence and abstention status
- Features or feature-set version
- Calibration and drift metrics
- Counterfactual outcomes from shadow evaluation
- Objective weights for quality, cost, and latency

Operational dashboards should expose route share, cost per request, quality by route, fallback rate, and changes relative to a stable baseline.

## 5. Fallback Strategy

A production router should use a layered fallback path:

1. **Pre-routing hard constraints**  
   Apply compliance, residency, safety, context-window, tenant, and budget restrictions before any learned decision.

2. **Primary routing decision**  
   Execute deterministic rules or select among eligible models using the learned router.

3. **Router failure or uncertainty**  
   If routing times out, required features are missing, confidence is below threshold, or the router is unhealthy, use a deterministic default model.

4. **Model execution failure**  
   Retry only when the error is transient and the operation is safe. Otherwise fail over to an explicitly compatible model with adequate context and capability.

5. **Quality-sensitive escalation**  
   Escalate to a stronger model only for defined signals, such as failed validation, tool-use errors, or low verifier confidence. Cap escalation attempts and total spend.

6. **Circuit breakers and kill switches**  
   Disable a model or learned router automatically when error, latency, cost, or quality thresholds are breached.

Fallbacks should avoid unbounded retry chains. Set maximum attempts, maximum cumulative latency, and a per-request cost ceiling.

## 6. Recommendation for a Cost-Sensitive, High-Volume Workload

Use a **deterministic, policy-based router as the production control plane**, optionally augmented by a constrained learned router after sufficient evaluation.

Recommended architecture:

- Route obvious low-complexity traffic to the cheapest acceptable model using explicit rules.
- Reserve expensive models for clearly defined task classes, premium tiers, or validated escalation conditions.
- Enforce per-request and aggregate budget limits independently of the router.
- Introduce a learned router initially in shadow mode to measure incremental savings and quality.
- If it demonstrates stable benefit, allow it to choose only within a deterministic eligibility set and cost envelope.
- Require abstention to a deterministic default when confidence is low or features are unavailable.
- Maintain route-share caps, canary deployment, circuit breakers, and instant rollback.

### Rationale

For high-volume workloads, even a small routing-distribution error can create a large cost increase. Deterministic routing offers stronger spend predictability, simpler auditing, and more reliable failure handling. Learned routing can improve efficiency by identifying requests that cheaper models can handle, but it should not control budgets, compliance, or unconstrained escalation.

**Bottom line:** begin with deterministic routing for predictable economics and operational safety. Add learned routing only as a bounded optimization layer, not as the sole authority.

# Technical Brief: Deterministic vs. Learned Model Routing

## 1. Definitions

**Deterministic policy-based routing** selects a model using explicit rules such as request type, customer tier, token count, latency target, language, risk class, or budget.

```text
if safety_risk == high: use reviewed high-capability model
elif task == classification: use small model
elif context_tokens > 32k: use long-context model
else: use standard model
```

**Learned automatic routing** uses a trained classifier, scoring model, bandit, or cascade to predict which model can satisfy a request at the lowest expected cost or latency. It may use prompt features, model confidence, historical outcomes, or online feedback.

---

## 2. Comparison

| Dimension | Deterministic Policy Routing | Learned Automatic Routing |
|---|---|---|
| **Controllability** | High. Behavior is explicit, reviewable, and easy to constrain by tenant, task, or risk level. | Lower. Decisions depend on learned correlations and may change after retraining or online adaptation. Requires hard constraints around the router. |
| **Cost predictability** | High. Traffic allocation and unit economics can be modeled directly, though broad rules may overuse expensive models. | Potentially better average cost, but less predictable. Distribution shifts or poor calibration can suddenly increase escalation rates or quality failures. |
| **Quality efficiency** | Coarse-grained. Rules may miss subtle prompt difficulty and route easy requests to oversized models. | Fine-grained. Can identify easy requests within otherwise difficult categories and improve the cost-quality frontier. |
| **Operational complexity** | Low to moderate. Requires policy maintenance, testing, and version control. | High. Requires labeled outcomes, training pipelines, calibration, drift detection, experiments, and rollback support. |
| **Auditability** | Strong. Each decision can be explained by a matched rule and policy version. | Weaker unless feature attribution, router scores, thresholds, and model versions are logged. |
| **Adaptability** | Changes require deliberate policy updates. Stable but slower to respond. | Can adapt to new traffic and model performance, but retraining can introduce regressions. |
| **Cold-start behavior** | Good if domain knowledge supports sensible rules. | Weak without representative labels or reliable proxy metrics. |
| **Compliance and isolation** | Straightforward to enforce data residency, approved-model lists, and customer-specific restrictions. | Unsafe as the sole control plane; compliance constraints should remain deterministic. |

---

## 3. Failure Modes

### Deterministic routing

- **Rule gaps:** New request types fall into an inappropriate default route.
- **Rule conflicts:** Overlapping policies produce unexpected precedence behavior.
- **Threshold cliffs:** Small input changes, such as crossing a token limit, cause large cost or quality changes.
- **Policy sprawl:** Accumulated exceptions become difficult to reason about.
- **Static misallocation:** Rules fail to reflect changing model capabilities, pricing, or traffic patterns.
- **Silent quality loss:** A cheap model may consistently underperform on a subset not represented in the rules.

**Mitigations:** policy linting, explicit precedence, shadow evaluation, bounded defaults, periodic traffic analysis, and versioned rollout.

### Learned routing

- **Distribution drift:** Production prompts differ from training data.
- **Miscalibration:** Router confidence does not correspond to actual success probability.
- **Proxy mismatch:** Optimizing ratings, confidence, or benchmark scores fails to optimize business outcomes.
- **Selective-label bias:** Outcomes are observed only for the model originally selected.
- **Router/model coupling:** A model upgrade invalidates learned routing boundaries.
- **Adversarial manipulation:** Prompt content influences routing to obtain a more expensive or less restricted model.
- **Feedback loops:** Online adaptation reinforces early routing mistakes.
- **Cost runaway:** Excessive uncertainty or changed traffic causes widespread escalation.
- **Correlated failure:** The router and selected model share weaknesses, making confidence-based fallback ineffective.

**Mitigations:** deterministic caps, randomized exploration, counterfactual evaluation, calibration monitoring, shadow traffic, drift alarms, and rapid rollback.

---

## 4. Observability Requirements

Both approaches should log:

- Request class and normalized workload attributes
- Router and policy version
- Candidate models and eligibility constraints
- Selected model and reason
- Input/output token usage
- Latency, errors, retries, and fallback path
- Estimated and actual cost
- Quality or task-success signals
- Safety and compliance outcomes

### Additional requirements for deterministic routing

- Matched rule and precedence chain
- Default-route frequency
- Traffic and cost per rule
- Rule coverage and conflict reports

### Additional requirements for learned routing

- Router score, confidence, and decision threshold
- Feature and training-data versions
- Calibration curves by workload segment
- Escalation and disagreement rates
- Drift metrics
- Counterfactual quality estimates from shadow or sampled evaluations
- Cost-quality frontier over time

Observability should support breakdowns by tenant, task, language, prompt length, risk level, model version, and router version. Aggregate averages can hide expensive or low-quality segments.

---

## 5. Fallback Strategy

A robust fallback system should be deterministic even when primary routing is learned.

1. **Eligibility filtering:** Remove models that violate compliance, context-window, modality, availability, or tenant constraints.
2. **Primary selection:** Apply policy rules or the learned router only within the eligible set.
3. **Execution fallback:** On timeout, rate limit, provider error, or malformed output, retry within a strict latency and cost budget.
4. **Quality escalation:** Escalate when confidence is low or validation fails—for example, schema validation, tool-execution checks, citation checks, or task-specific verifiers.
5. **Degraded mode:** If premium models are unavailable or a budget circuit breaker trips, use a designated lower-cost model with reduced functionality.
6. **Safe terminal response:** For high-risk tasks, abstain rather than silently downgrade below the required capability.
7. **Loop prevention:** Set maximum attempts, maximum cumulative tokens, and maximum spend per request.
8. **Emergency override:** Support instant pinning to a known model or policy version without retraining or redeployment.

Avoid relying only on the selected model’s self-reported confidence; it is often poorly calibrated and correlated with its own failures.

---

## 6. Recommendation for a Cost-Sensitive, High-Volume Workload

Use a **hybrid architecture with deterministic guardrails and learned optimization inside those guardrails**.

### Recommended design

- Use deterministic policies for:
  - Compliance and data residency
  - Safety-critical or high-value requests
  - Tenant entitlements
  - Hard latency and spend limits
  - Context-window and modality requirements
  - Provider outages and degraded modes
- Use learned routing for:
  - Choosing among eligible models
  - Predicting whether the lowest-cost model will meet a defined quality threshold
  - Escalating difficult requests to stronger models
- Default to the least expensive qualified model.
- Require the learned router to justify escalation through a calibrated expected-quality or expected-loss threshold.
- Enforce per-request and aggregate budget circuit breakers.
- Sample traffic to stronger models for counterfactual evaluation and drift detection.
- Roll out through shadow mode, then small canaries, with deterministic rollback.

### Decision objective

Optimize expected total loss rather than model price alone:

\[
\text{Expected loss} =
\text{inference cost}
+ \lambda_q \cdot \text{quality-failure cost}
+ \lambda_l \cdot \text{latency cost}
+ \lambda_r \cdot \text{risk cost}
\]

For high volume, even a small routing improvement can produce substantial savings. However, a fully learned router introduces unacceptable cost and operational variance unless bounded by explicit policies. The hybrid approach provides most of the economic benefit of automatic routing while preserving auditability, predictable worst-case spend, compliance, and rapid recovery.

### Deterministic routing

Common failures include:

- **Rule gaps:** New request types do not match an appropriate policy.
- **Threshold cliffs:** Small input changes cause disproportionate routing changes.
- **Policy conflicts:** Multiple rules match, producing ambiguous precedence.
- **Stale assumptions:** Rules continue routing to models whose cost or quality profile has changed.
- **Combinatorial complexity:** Policies become difficult to maintain as models, tenants, and exceptions multiply.
- **Systematic under-routing:** Difficult requests are sent to inexpensive models because complexity is not visible in metadata.

### Learned routing

Common failures include:

- **Distribution drift:** Production traffic differs from router training data.
- **Miscalibration:** Confidence scores do not correspond to actual downstream quality.
- **Biased labels:** Training data favors certain domains, languages, request lengths, or premium models.
- **Correlated failure:** The router selects a model based on signals that also predict that model’s weakness.
- **Feedback loops:** Only routed-model outcomes are observed, limiting counterfactual learning.
- **Cost excursions:** A threshold or feature shift routes excessive volume to expensive models.
- **Router outage or latency:** Routing inference becomes an additional dependency on the critical path.
- **Exploration risk:** Online learning sends production requests to insufficient models to gather data.

Mitigations include hard routing constraints, calibrated confidence thresholds, offline replay, shadow deployment, capped exploration, spend limits, drift detection, and deterministic fallback.

Both approaches should record:

- Request class and relevant non-sensitive features
- Selected model, model version, and provider
- Routing reason or score
- Estimated and actual input/output tokens
- Cost, latency, retries, and error status
- Quality signals such as task success, user feedback, or evaluator score
- Fallback and escalation events
- Policy or router version

Additional requirements for learned routing include:

- Confidence and calibration metrics
- Quality and cost by score bucket
- Feature and label drift
- Route allocation by tenant, language, domain, and task type
- Counterfactual or sampled evaluations across alternative models
- Regret relative to a quality-constrained cost baseline

Operational dashboards should expose p50/p95/p99 latency, cost per successful request, premium-model utilization, fallback rate, quality-target violation rate, and route-distribution changes.

## 5. Fallback Strategy

A robust routing hierarchy should separate **eligibility**, **optimization**, and **recovery**:

1. **Hard eligibility rules**
   - Enforce safety, data residency, context-window, modality, tenant, and SLA constraints.
2. **Primary routing decision**
   - Apply deterministic policy or a learned selector only among eligible models.
3. **Confidence handling**
   - If the learned router is unavailable, out of distribution, or below a confidence threshold, use a deterministic route.
4. **Execution recovery**
   - On timeout, rate limit, or provider failure, retry only where safe, then fail over to a compatible model or provider.
5. **Quality escalation**
   - Escalate to a more capable model when validation fails, tool execution fails, or the first model reports low confidence.
6. **Budget guardrails**
   - Cap premium-model traffic, per-request cost, retries, and escalation depth.
7. **Terminal behavior**
   - Fail explicitly rather than silently routing to a model that violates safety, residency, or minimum-quality requirements.

Fallbacks should be acyclic, bounded, idempotency-aware, and tested under provider outages and quota exhaustion.

## 6. Recommendation for a Cost-Sensitive, High-Volume Workload

Use a **constrained hybrid architecture**, beginning with deterministic routing and introducing learned routing only inside strict policy boundaries.

Recommended design:

- Use deterministic rules for compliance, modality, context limits, contractual SLAs, safety-sensitive tasks, and maximum spend.
- Route well-understood, repetitive traffic directly to inexpensive models.
- Use a calibrated learned router for ambiguous requests where model choice materially affects cost.
- Require the learned router to select from a policy-approved candidate set.
- Default to the least expensive model expected to meet the quality target.
- Escalate only after a confidence, validation, or execution failure.
- Set premium-route quotas and automatic circuit breakers for cost or quality anomalies.
- Keep a deterministic router available as the immediate rollback and outage fallback.
- Validate changes through offline replay, shadow traffic, and small canary deployments before increasing allocation.

### Bottom line

For high-volume, cost-sensitive production, fully learned routing introduces unnecessary budget and operational risk unless traffic is diverse enough to justify it and reliable quality labels exist. A deterministic foundation provides predictable spend, auditability, and safe recovery. A bounded learned component can then reduce over-routing to expensive models and improve quality on difficult requests without surrendering operational control.

### Contradictions

- **Current-event accuracy vs. no external services:** Current events change after the assistant’s training or last local update. Without live data sources, it cannot reliably know or verify them.
- **Instant response vs. guaranteed accuracy:** Verification, retrieval, and conflict resolution take time. Requiring zero latency prevents adequate validation.
- **“Always” guarantees:** Network conditions, hardware failures, ambiguous reports, misinformation, and rapidly changing facts make absolute availability and accuracy impossible.

### Why they cannot all hold

The assistant can respond instantly using only stored knowledge, but that knowledge may be stale. It can improve current-event accuracy by consulting authoritative sources, but that violates the external-service restriction and introduces latency. Thus, all three guarantees cannot be satisfied simultaneously.

### Revised requirements

1. The assistant must begin responding within a defined latency target, such as **500 ms under normal operating conditions**.
2. For current events, it may use **approved authoritative external sources** and must cite them and include retrieval timestamps.
3. If external access is unavailable or prohibited, it must:
   - disclose its knowledge cutoff or last local update,
   - avoid presenting unverified current information as fact, and
   - state when it cannot confirm an event.
4. Accuracy should be defined as a **measurable target**, not an absolute guarantee—for example, a specified benchmark accuracy rate with documented correction procedures.
5. Answers involving evolving events must distinguish **confirmed facts, disputed claims, and uncertainty**.

### Revised requirement set

1. **Latency:** Return an initial response within a defined target, such as 500 ms for 95% of requests.
2. **Freshness:** Clearly state the knowledge cutoff or timestamp of the most recent locally available data.
3. **Current events:**  
   - If external access is prohibited, do not claim real-time accuracy; explain that recent developments may be missing.  
   - If current accuracy is required, permit access to approved, auditable data sources.
4. **Accuracy:** Provide the best-supported answer available, distinguish confirmed facts from preliminary reports, and express uncertainty when verification is incomplete.
5. **Failure behavior:** Never fabricate missing updates. If reliable current information is unavailable, say so and provide the latest known information with its date.
6. **Verification trade-off:** Allow additional time for high-risk or fast-changing topics where corroboration is necessary.

### Contradictions

- **“Always accurate on current events” vs. “without calling external services”**: Current events change continuously. Without access to live or periodically updated data, the assistant’s knowledge becomes stale and cannot guarantee accuracy.
- **“Always respond instantly” vs. accuracy**: Verification, reasoning, and source comparison take time. A strict zero-latency response cannot also guarantee correctness.
- **Use of “always”**: Absolute guarantees are impossible because of ambiguous reports, conflicting sources, outages, incomplete information, and newly unfolding events.

### Revised requirement set

1. Respond within a defined latency target, such as **95% of requests within two seconds**.
2. Use only locally available information when external services are prohibited.
3. Clearly state the **knowledge cutoff or last synchronization time** for current-event questions.
4. Do not claim current accuracy when information may be stale; explicitly communicate uncertainty.
5. If verified live information is required, permit access to approved external sources with defined timeout, privacy, and reliability controls.
6. Target measurable accuracy on a maintained evaluation set rather than guaranteeing perfect accuracy.

A concise replacement could be:

> “The assistant should respond within two seconds for at least 95% of requests. When external access is disabled, it must answer using locally available data, disclose its last update time, and flag information that may be outdated. For verified current-event answers, it may query approved external sources and must cite them.”
